The test set must stay unseen

The Tatoeba test set was cut from the same pool of sentences as our training data. If a test sentence also appears in training, the model can recite the answer and the test score stops measuring translation. This problem, contamination, is one that large-model papers take seriously: the GPT-4 technical report has a whole appendix of contamination checks for its benchmarks.

Comparing exact strings is not enough: Хватит! and хватит. are the same sentence for our purposes. We compare fingerprints instead: lowercase, without punctuation and spaces, and with ё read as е (Russian texts use the two letters interchangeably).

def fingerprint(text):
    text = text.casefold()  # lowercase that also handles special cases like ß
    text = text.replace("ё", "е")
    return re.sub(r"[\W_]+", "", text)  # drop everything that is not a letter or a digit


print(fingerprint("Хватит!"), fingerprint("хватит."), fingerprint("Ты безнадёжна!"))

хватит хватит тыбезнадежна

A training pair leaks when its English or its Russian sentence has the fingerprint of a test sentence. Compare the two ways of checking:

test_en_prints = set(test.en.map(fingerprint))
test_ru_prints = set(test.ru.map(fingerprint))

exact_en = train.en.isin(set(test.en))
exact_ru = train.ru.isin(set(test.ru))
print("pairs that share a sentence with the test set")

printed_en = train.en.map(fingerprint).isin(test_en_prints)
printed_ru = train.ru.map(fingerprint).isin(test_ru_prints)

A validation split that doesn’t leak

We also need a validation set: data the model never trains on, used to choose settings and to stop training at the right moment. The usual move is to hold out a random 2% of the pairs. Here that would be a mistake, and the picture shows why.

These are real pairs from our data. Think of every sentence as a node and every translation pair as an edge. A random split cuts edges independently, so a validation pair like Cut it out! → Прекрати! still has both of its sentences in training pairs. The model has seen the source and has learned to produce the target, and validation would reward memory.

The fix is to split whole connected components: groups of sentences linked by translation, directly or through each other. A classic data structure finds them, union–find. Every sentence starts as a group of its own. Every pair says “these two sentences belong together”, and we merge their groups. To tell whether two sentences are already in one group, each group has a representative, its root: every sentence keeps a link to a “parent” sentence, and following the parents leads to the root.

class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self):
        self.parent = {}  # sentence -> its parent; a root is its own parent

    def find(self, x):
        if x not in self.parent:
            self.parent[x] = x  # a sentence seen for the first time is a group of one

        root = x
        while self.parent[root] != root:
            root = self.parent[root]

        # path compression: point everything on the way straight at the root
        while self.parent[x] != root:
            next_x = self.parent[x]
            self.parent[x] = root
            x = next_x
        return root

    def union(self, a, b):
        root_a = self.find(a)
        root_b = self.find(b)
        if root_a != root_b:
            self.parent[root_a] = root_b  # the two groups become one

The second loop in find is what keeps it fast. Without it, a chain of parents can grow long, and every lookup walks the whole chain. With it, a lookup shortens the chain for everyone after it:

That is the actual state of the structure halfway through the example below. A sentence is stored together with its language, ("en", "Stop it."), because the same string can occur on both sides (names, numbers). Run it on the pairs from the pictures, plus one unrelated pair:

for en, ru in example_pairs:

All eight pairs from the picture end up in one group, and the unrelated pair forms its own.

With path compression alone, \(m\) operations on \(n\) sentences cost \(O(m \log n)\) in the worst case. Also attaching the smaller group under the larger one (union by rank) gives the famous near-linear bound \(O(m\,\alpha(n))\), where \(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function, which stays below 5 for any \(n\) that fits in our universe (Tarjan, 1975). For our data compression alone is plenty. Now the real thing: every training pair, and a group label for each.

start = time.perf_counter()

groups = UnionFind()
for en, ru in zip(train.en, train.ru):
    groups.union(("en", en), ("ru", ru))

labels = []
for en in train.en:
    root = groups.find(("en", en))
    labels.append(str(root))  # a pair is labeled with the root of its group
train = train.assign(group=labels)
print("done in", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1), "s")

group_sizes = train.groupby("group").size()
print("groups:", len(group_sizes))
print("groups with more than one pair:", (group_sizes > 1).sum())
print("pairs in the largest group:", group_sizes.max())

The largest group is a whole family of ways to tell someone to stop, or to go away. A few of its English and Russian sentences:

largest = train[train.group == group_sizes.idxmax()]

Now compare the two ways of splitting. leak_rate measures the share of validation pairs whose English or Russian sentence also occurs somewhere in training:

def leak_rate(train_part, valid_part):
    seen_english = set(train_part.en)
    seen_russian = set(train_part.ru)
    leaked = valid_part.en.isin(seen_english) | valid_part.ru.isin(seen_russian)
    return leaked.mean()

First the random split: every pair goes to validation with probability 2%.

VAL_SHARE = 0.02
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

random_valid = rng.random(len(train)) < VAL_SHARE
random_leak = leak_rate(train[~random_valid], train[random_valid])
print(f"random split: {random_leak:.1%} of validation pairs leak")

random split: 57.2% of validation pairs leak

Then the split by groups: we pick 2% of the groups, and their pairs, all of them, go to validation.

all_groups = train.group.unique()
n_valid_groups = int(VAL_SHARE * len(all_groups))
valid_groups = rng.choice(all_groups, size=n_valid_groups, replace=False)

train = train[~in_valid].drop(columns="group")

print(f"split by groups: {group_leak:.1%} of validation pairs leak")

Split by whatever must not be shared. Here that’s sentences, so we split by groups of linked sentences; for medical images it would be patients, for code it would be repositories.

The splits are final. We save them; at the end of the lesson they are published, so that lesson 2 can start from exactly these sentences.

3. Why not words, and why not characters

Two designs come to mind before BPE does: one token per word, or one token per character. Both have been used, and both fail in instructive ways.

A word tokenizer gives each distinct word an id. Its problem is that the number of distinct words never stops growing. Watch it grow as we read through the training data, recording the number of distinct words after every thousand words read:

WORD = re.compile(r"\w+")  # a run of letters or digits


def vocabulary_growth(sentences, every=1_000):
    seen = set()
    words_read = 0
    n_points, v_points = [], []
    for sentence in sentences:
        for word in WORD.findall(sentence.lower()):
            seen.add(word)
            words_read += 1
            if words_read % every == 0:
                n_points.append(words_read)
                v_points.append(len(seen))
    return np.array(n_points), np.array(v_points)


shuffled = train.sample(frac=1, random_state=SEED)
growth = {"en": vocabulary_growth(shuffled.en), "ru": vocabulary_growth(shuffled.ru)}

Empirically, vocabulary growth follows Heaps’ law:

\[V(N) = K N^{\beta}, \qquad 0 < \beta < 1,\]

where \(N\) is the number of words read, \(V(N)\) the number of distinct words among them, and \(K\), \(\beta\) constants of the language and the text. \(\beta\) is the interesting one: it says how fast new word forms keep appearing. With \(\beta = 0.5\), reading four times more text doubles the vocabulary.

Taking logarithms turns the law into a straight line, \(\log V = \log K + \beta \log N\), so we can estimate \(\beta\) as the slope of a least-squares line through the points in log–log coordinates; np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

for lang, color in [("en", COLORS["enc"]), ("ru", COLORS["dec"])]:
    n, v = growth[lang]
    beta, log_k = np.polyfit(np.log(n), np.log(v), 1)
    label = f"{lang}: β = {beta:.2f}, {v[-1]:,} distinct words"
    ax.loglog(n, v, color=color, label=label)
    fitted = np.exp(log_k) * n**beta  # the fitted law, dashed
    ax.loglog(n, fitted, color=color, linestyle=(0, (2, 3)), linewidth=1.2)

ax.set_xlabel("words read, N")
ax.set_ylabel("distinct words, V(N)")
ax.set_title("Russian keeps producing new word forms")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()

Russian grows faster and ends with several times more distinct words, although the Russian side has fewer words in total. The reason is morphology: понимать, понимаю, понимаешь, понимание, недопонимание, понимания, … are all different strings to a word tokenizer, while English mostly reuses understand.

The other side of the same coin is the long tail. Count how many distinct words occur exactly once in all of the training data (linguists call them hapax legomena, “said once”):

word_freqs = {}
for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for sentence in train[lang]:
        counts.update(WORD.findall(sentence.lower()))
    word_freqs[lang] = counts

    seen_once = 0
    for count in counts.values():
        if count == 1:
            seen_once += 1
    print(f"{lang}: {seen_once / len(counts):.0%} of distinct words occur once")

en: 33% of distinct words occur once
ru: 42% of distinct words occur once

A large share of the vocabulary is words the model would see once in all of training, too rarely to learn anything about them. A real vocabulary has to stop somewhere anyway. Keep the 30 000 most frequent training words and count how many validation words fall outside, the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate:

def oov_rate(counts, valid_sentences, size=30_000):
    vocabulary = set()
    for word, _ in counts.most_common(size):
        vocabulary.add(word)

    total, unknown = 0, 0
    for sentence in valid_sentences:
        for word in WORD.findall(sentence.lower()):
            total += 1
            if word not in vocabulary:
                unknown += 1
    return unknown / total


for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    rate = oov_rate(word_freqs[lang], valid[lang])
    print(f"{lang}: {rate:.2%} of validation words are unknown")

en: 0.35% of validation words are unknown
ru: 3.33% of validation words are unknown

Every unknown word becomes the same placeholder, and the model can neither read nor write it. For Russian that happens an order of magnitude more often than for English, and those are exactly the rare inflected forms a translator must produce.

The opposite extreme, one token per character, has no unknown words at all, but the sequences get long:

for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    chars = valid[lang].str.len().mean()
    words = word_count(valid[lang]).mean()
    print(f"{lang}: {chars:.1f} characters, {words:.1f} words per sentence;")
    print(f"    {chars / words:.1f} times longer in characters")

en: 31.0 characters, 6.2 words per sentence;
    5.0 times longer in characters
ru: 31.0 characters, 5.4 words per sentence;
    5.7 times longer in characters

Length is expensive. In lesson 2 you will see that self-attention compares every position with every other, so its cost grows with the square of the sequence length \(T\):

\[\text{cost} \propto T^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\text{cost}_{\text{chars}}}{\text{cost}_{\text{words}}} = \left(\frac{T_{\text{chars}}}{T_{\text{words}}}\right)^2.\]

Sequences \(k\) times longer make attention \(k^2\) times more expensive: with the ratios above, a character model pays for attention dozens of times more than a word model, and it has to learn spelling before it can learn meaning.

Subword tokenization is the compromise: frequent words stay whole, rare words are split into frequent pieces, and every string can still be written with the basic alphabet. Byte-pair encoding is the most widely used way to find those pieces.

4. BPE from scratch

BPE was invented in 1994 by Philip Gage as a way to compress files: find the most common pair of adjacent bytes, replace it everywhere with a byte value the file doesn’t use, repeat. In 2016 Sennrich, Haddow and Birch noticed that the same procedure, run on the letters of words, finds good subword units for translation. Today it builds the tokenizers of GPT-2, GPT-4o, Llama 3 and DeepSeek-V3, all of which you took apart in section 1.

The idea fits in one picture:

Start with every word spelled out as single characters. Then repeat: find the pair of adjacent symbols that occurs most often in the corpus, merge it into one new symbol everywhere, and add that symbol to the vocabulary. Frequent words end up as one symbol, because merging their pieces paid off again and again; rare words stay split into pieces that other words share.

Formally, let \(f(w)\) be the frequency of word \(w\) in the corpus and \(n_{ab}(w)\) the number of times symbol \(a\) is immediately followed by symbol \(b\) in the current spelling of \(w\). The frequency of the pair is

\[c(a, b) = \sum_{w} f(w)\, n_{ab}(w),\]

and each step merges

\[(a^*, b^*) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{(a, b)} c(a, b).\]

If two pairs are equally frequent we take the one that compares greater as a pair of Python strings, that is, by Unicode code points. Any fixed rule works; what matters is that it is deterministic, so the same corpus always yields the same tokenizer. After \(M\) merges the vocabulary holds the initial alphabet \(\Sigma\) plus one symbol per merge: \(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert = \lvert\Sigma\rvert + M\).

Pre-tokenization

Merges never cross word boundaries, so we first split text into words and punctuation. A word keeps the space in front of it, written as ▁ (the convention of SentencePiece, Kudo and Richardson, 2018). It’s the same trick you saw in GPT-4o’s ␣strawberry: with the spaces inside the tokens, decoding is plain concatenation, and the model can tell the beginning of a word from the middle of one.

The regular expression has two alternatives:  ?\w+ is an optional space followed by letters or digits, and  ?[^\w\s]+ is an optional space followed by punctuation (anything that is neither a word character nor whitespace).

PRE_TOKEN = re.compile(r" ?\w+| ?[^\w\s]+")


def pretokenize(text):
    pieces = PRE_TOKEN.findall(" " + text)  # the leading space marks the first word too
    return [piece.replace(" ", "▁") for piece in pieces]


print(pretokenize(RU_EXAMPLE))
print(pretokenize("Let's go — now!"))

['▁Исследовательница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вымоталась', '.']
['▁Let', "'", 's', '▁go', '▁—', '▁now', '!']

Counting pairs on a toy corpus

Before touching half a million sentences, run every step on three Russian words whose counts you can check by hand. A word is stored as a tuple of its symbols, with its frequency:

toy = {
    tuple("▁понимание"): 5,
    tuple("▁недопонимание"): 3,
    tuple("▁понимать"): 4,
}


def pair_counts(words):
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for word, freq in words.items():
        for left, right in zip(word, word[1:]):  # every adjacent pair in the word
            counts[left, right] += freq
    return counts


pair_counts(toy).most_common(5)

[(('н', 'и'), 20),
 (('п', 'о'), 12),
 (('о', 'н'), 12),
 (('и', 'м'), 12),
 (('м', 'а'), 12)]

н + и wins: it occurs twice in понимание (five times), twice in недопонимание (three times) and once in понимать (four times), which gives \(2 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4 = 20\), the formula for \(c(a, b)\) above.

Picking the winner, with our rule for ties:

def most_frequent_pair(counts):
    best_pair, best_count = None, 0
    for pair, count in counts.items():
        if count > best_count or (count == best_count and pair > best_pair):
            best_pair, best_count = pair, count
    return best_pair


most_frequent_pair(pair_counts(toy))

('н', 'и')

Merging a pair rewrites a word, scanning it from left to right:

def merge_word(word, pair):
    merged = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(word):
        if i + 1 < len(word) and (word[i], word[i + 1]) == pair:
            merged.append(word[i] + word[i + 1])  # two symbols become one
            i += 2
        else:
            merged.append(word[i])
            i += 1
    return tuple(merged)


before = tuple("▁недопонимание")
after = merge_word(before, ("н", "и"))
token_chips([before, after], labels=["before", "after"])
plt.show()

The straightforward trainer

Training is these three steps in a loop:

def train_bpe_simple(words, n_merges):
    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        counts = pair_counts(words)
        if not counts:  # every word is a single symbol, nothing left to merge
            break
        pair = most_frequent_pair(counts)
        merges.append(pair)

        merged_words = {}
        for word, freq in words.items():
            merged_words[merge_word(word, pair)] = freq
        words = merged_words
    return merges


train_bpe_simple(toy, 6)

[('н', 'и'),
 ('п', 'о'),
 ('по', 'ни'),
 ('пони', 'м'),
 ('поним', 'а'),
 ('▁', 'понима')]

Six merges on the toy corpus, each one built on the previous ones: ни, then по, then по + ни = пони, and so on until the whole stem ▁понима. Now a real sample: we count the words of 40 000 sentences, English and Russian together, and run 300 merges.

def word_counts(sentences):
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for sentence in sentences:
        counts.update(pretokenize(sentence))

    words = {}
    for word, freq in counts.items():
        words[tuple(word)] = freq
    return words


SAMPLE_SENTENCES = 40_000
SAMPLE_MERGES = 300

sample = pd.concat([train.en, train.ru]).sample(SAMPLE_SENTENCES, random_state=SEED)
sample_words = word_counts(sample)
print("distinct words in the sample:", len(sample_words))

start = time.perf_counter()
simple_merges = train_bpe_simple(sample_words, SAMPLE_MERGES)
simple_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
print(len(simple_merges), "merges in", round(simple_seconds, 1), "s")

distinct words in the sample: 23926
300 merges in 12.0 s

The first merges are the most frequent pieces of both languages, interleaved:

first_30 = ["".join(pair) for pair in simple_merges[:30]]
token_chips(
    [first_30[0:10], first_30[10:20], first_30[20:30]],
    labels=["merges 1–10", "11–20", "21–30"],
)
plt.show()

Word starts like ▁t, ▁н, ▁п come first, then frequent syllables and whole short words. ▁T seems to appear twice in the second row: one is the Latin T, the other the Cyrillic Т that starts Том. They look identical and are different characters, which is why we never compare text by how it looks.

The trainer is correct but slow. Every merge recounts all pairs in all words, so the cost is \(O(M \cdot L)\), where \(L\) is the total number of symbols in all distinct words. Both factors grow for the real run: the full training set has several times more distinct words than this sample, and we want thousands of merges, not hundreds.

The incremental trainer

Most of that recounting is wasted, because a merge changes very little. Take one word of the toy corpus and compare its pairs before and after merging н + и:

Only the pairs that touch the merge change, and only in words that contain the pair. So instead of recounting, we keep two tables between steps:

  • pair_freq: how often each pair occurs in the corpus, \(c(a, b)\);
  • words_with_pair: for each pair, which words contain it.

After a merge we visit only the affected words. For each of them, remove_pairs takes all its pairs out of the tables, the word is rewritten, and add_pairs puts its new pairs back. Removing and re-adding the whole word is simpler than computing the exact difference, and the result is the same: the pairs that didn’t change go out and come back with the same count.

def train_bpe(word_freqs, n_merges):
    words = [list(word) for word in word_freqs]  # current spelling of every word
    freqs = list(word_freqs.values())
    pair_freq = collections.Counter()
    words_with_pair = collections.defaultdict(set)  # pair -> indices of words with it

    def add_pairs(i):
        for pair in zip(words[i], words[i][1:]):
            pair_freq[pair] += freqs[i]
            words_with_pair[pair].add(i)

    def remove_pairs(i):
        for pair in zip(words[i], words[i][1:]):
            pair_freq[pair] -= freqs[i]
            if pair_freq[pair] == 0:
                del pair_freq[pair]
            words_with_pair[pair].discard(i)

    for i in range(len(words)):
        add_pairs(i)

    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        if not pair_freq:
            break
        pair = most_frequent_pair(pair_freq)
        merges.append(pair)
        for i in list(words_with_pair[pair]):  # only the words that contain the pair change
            remove_pairs(i)
            words[i] = list(merge_word(words[i], pair))
            add_pairs(i)

    final_spelling = {}
    for word, spelling in zip(word_freqs, words):
        final_spelling[word] = tuple(spelling)
    return merges, final_spelling

A faster algorithm is only useful if it computes the same thing. Same input, same number of merges:

start = time.perf_counter()
fast_merges, _ = train_bpe(sample_words, SAMPLE_MERGES)
fast_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

assert fast_merges == simple_merges
print("identical merges")
print("simple:", round(simple_seconds, 1), "s, incremental:", round(fast_seconds, 2), "s")
print(round(simple_seconds / fast_seconds), "times faster")

identical merges
simple: 12.0 s, incremental: 0.46 s
26 times faster

Now the full training set, both languages together, and 8 000 merges. One shared vocabulary for English and Russian lets the model share one embedding table between encoder and decoder later on, and the two languages have more in common than their alphabets suggest: digits, punctuation, names, borrowed words.

N_MERGES = 8_000
all_words = word_counts(pd.concat([train.en, train.ru]))

start = time.perf_counter()
merges, segmentation = train_bpe(all_words, N_MERGES)
seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - start)
print(len(merges), "merges over", len(all_words), "distinct words in", seconds, "s")

alphabet = set()
for word in all_words:
    alphabet.update(word)
vocabulary_size = len(alphabet) + len(merges)
print("vocabulary:", len(alphabet), "characters +", len(merges), "merges")
print("          =", vocabulary_size, "symbols")

8000 merges over 119567 distinct words in 15 s
vocabulary: 242 characters + 8000 merges
          = 8242 symbols

Encoding: replay the merges in order

To tokenize new text we don’t count anything. We apply the learned merges in the order they were learned: in each word, find the adjacent pair that was merged earliest during training, its rank, merge it, and repeat until no adjacent pair is in the merge table. Ranks matter because merges build on each other: ▁недо exists only because ▁н, ▁не and до were merged first.

ranks = {}
for rank, pair in enumerate(merges):
    ranks[pair] = rank  # pair -> when it was merged: 0, 1, 2, ...


def encode_word(word, ranks, steps=None):
    symbols = list(word)
    while True:
        # find the adjacent pair with the lowest rank
        best_i, best_rank = None, None
        for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):
            rank = ranks.get((symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]))
            if rank is not None and (best_rank is None or rank < best_rank):
                best_i, best_rank = i, rank

        if best_i is None:  # no pair left that training ever merged
            return symbols

        symbols[best_i : best_i + 2] = [symbols[best_i] + symbols[best_i + 1]]
        if steps is not None:
            steps.append((list(symbols), best_i))  # remember every step, to draw it below


steps = []
encode_word("▁недопонимание", ranks, steps)
rows = [symbols for symbols, _ in steps]
token_chips(rows, strong=lambda row, col, _: col == steps[row][1], size=11)
plt.show()

Each row is one merge; the highlighted symbol is the one just created. Replaying merges by rank should reproduce exactly the segmentation that training arrived at. Rather than believe it, check it for every word in the training data:

mismatches = []
for word, trained in segmentation.items():
    if encode_word("".join(word), ranks) != list(trained):
        mismatches.append(word)

assert not mismatches, mismatches[:5]
print("encoding reproduces the training segmentation for all", len(segmentation), "words")

encoding reproduces the training segmentation for all 119567 words

Encoding a sentence is pre-tokenization plus encode_word, and decoding is concatenation with ▁ turned back into spaces. Nothing is lost on the way; the round trip over the whole validation set confirms it:

def encode(text):
    tokens = []
    for word in pretokenize(text):
        tokens.extend(encode_word(word, ranks))
    return tokens


def decode(tokens):
    text = "".join(tokens).replace("▁", " ")
    return text[1:]  # drop the space we added in front of the first word


for sentence in pd.concat([valid.en, valid.ru]):
    assert decode(encode(sentence)) == sentence

print(encode(RU_EXAMPLE))

['▁И', 'сс', 'ледо', 'ва', 'тель', 'ница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вы', 'мо', 'т', 'алась', '.']

What the merges learned

Nobody told BPE about prefixes or suffixes, yet some appear on their own, because a frequent morpheme is a frequent string:

words = [
    "▁misunderstanding",
    "▁недопонимание",
    "▁исследовательница",
    "▁вымоталась",
    "▁researcher",
    "▁untranslatable",
]
segmented = [encode_word(word, ranks) for word in words]
token_chips(segmented, labels=[word[1:] for word in words], size=11)
plt.show()

Some splits look like a linguist’s: недо, or the feminine suffix ница, the piece that turns исследователь (a researcher) into a woman researcher. Others don’t (st + and). BPE optimizes frequency, not meaning. The model will learn what the pieces mean from context; what the tokenizer controls is that frequent things are short and every rare thing can still be spelled.

5. The production tokenizer

Our implementation is readable and correct. It would also be slow at serving time and easy to break: the normalization lives in one function, the pre-tokenization in another, and nothing forces a server to call them the same way as training did. Hugging Face tokenizers, written in Rust, packs the whole pipeline into one object that is saved as one file:

The tokenizers of section 1 are such files; you downloaded five of them. The rule we follow:

The tokenizer owns its normalization. Then training, evaluation and the deployed service can’t normalize differently, because there is no separate step to forget.

First the normalizer, rebuilt from the same choices as normalize, step for step:

hf_normalizer = normalizers.Sequence(
    [
        normalizers.NFKC(),
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\p{Mn}"), ""),  # combining marks
        *[normalizers.Replace(fancy, plain) for fancy, plain in QUOTES.items()],
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\s+-\s+"), " — "),
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\s+"), " "),
        normalizers.Strip(),
    ]
)

print(hf_normalizer.normalize_str("Он сказал:   «Я не знаю» - и ушёл…"))

Он сказал: "Я не знаю" — и ушёл...

“Rebuilt from the same choices” is a claim, so check it on every raw sentence we have:

raw_sentences = pd.concat([train_raw.en, train_raw.ru, test_raw.en, test_raw.ru])

different = []
for sentence in raw_sentences:
    if hf_normalizer.normalize_str(sentence) != normalize(sentence):
        different.append(sentence)

assert not different, different[:5]
print("identical normalization on all", len(raw_sentences), "raw sentences")

identical normalization on all 1156102 raw sentences

Then the pre-tokenizer: the same regular expression splits words and punctuation, and Metaspace turns the spaces into ▁. Regular-expression engines don’t always agree on what a “word character” is (Python’s and the Rust library’s disagree on combining marks and subscript digits), which is one more reason the normalizer removed those first. Check this one too:

hf_pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.Sequence(
    [
        pre_tokenizers.Split(Regex(r" ?\w+| ?[^\w\s]+"), behavior="isolated"),
        pre_tokenizers.Metaspace(replacement="▁", prepend_scheme="never", split=False),
    ]
)


def hf_pretokenize(text):
    pieces = hf_pre_tokenizer.pre_tokenize_str(" " + text)  # (piece, position) pairs
    return [piece for piece, _ in pieces]


normalized_sentences = pd.concat([train.en, train.ru, valid.en, valid.ru, test.en, test.ru])
for sentence in normalized_sentences:
    assert hf_pretokenize(sentence) == pretokenize(sentence), sentence
print("identical pre-tokenization on all", len(normalized_sentences), "sentences")

identical pre-tokenization on all 1109696 sentences

The tokenizer needs four special tokens, which the model will use from lesson 2 on: <pad> fills shorter sentences in a batch, <unk> stands for a character never seen in training, <bos> and <eos> mark the beginning and end of a sentence. They take ids 0 to 3.

<unk> is the price of starting from characters rather than bytes, as GPT-2 does: a character that never occurred in training (an emoji, a Chinese name) has no symbol. For a translator between two languages that is a fair trade; the tokens stay readable, and no letter gets cut in half.

SPECIAL_TOKENS = ["<pad>", "<unk>", "<bos>", "<eos>"]


def build_tokenizer(vocab_size):
    tokenizer = Tokenizer(models.BPE(unk_token="<unk>"))
    tokenizer.normalizer = normalizers.Sequence([hf_normalizer, normalizers.Prepend(" ")])
    tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = hf_pre_tokenizer
    tokenizer.decoder = decoders.Metaspace(
        replacement="▁", prepend_scheme="always", split=False
    )

    trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        special_tokens=SPECIAL_TOKENS,
        min_frequency=2,  # ignore pairs seen only once
        show_progress=False,
    )
    tokenizer.train_from_iterator(list(train.en) + list(train.ru), trainer)
    return tokenizer


VOCAB_SIZE = 16_000

start = time.perf_counter()
tokenizer = build_tokenizer(VOCAB_SIZE)
seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1)
print("vocabulary of", tokenizer.get_vocab_size(), "trained in", seconds, "s")
print(tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).tokens)

vocabulary of 16000 trained in 19.3 s
['▁И', 'сс', 'ледо', 'ватель', 'ница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вы', 'мот', 'алась', '.']

Compare the timings: the Rust trainer builds twice as many symbols in a fraction of the time our Python one needed for the same corpus. Both see exactly the same words, since we checked normalization and pre-tokenization, so their merges should agree except where the two implementations make different choices: Hugging Face breaks ties between equally frequent pairs differently, and skips pairs seen only once (min_frequency=2). The saved tokenizer lists its merges in order; compare the first thousand with ours:

saved = json.loads(tokenizer.to_str())

hf_merges = []
for merge in saved["model"]["merges"]:
    if isinstance(merge, str):  # older versions of tokenizers store a merge as "a b"
        merge = merge.split(" ")
    hf_merges.append(tuple(merge))

shared = set(hf_merges[:1000]) & set(merges[:1000])
print(len(shared), "of the first 1000 merges are the same in both")

first_difference = 0
while hf_merges[first_difference] == merges[first_difference]:
    first_difference += 1
print("the lists first differ at merge", first_difference + 1)
print("Hugging Face merged", hf_merges[first_difference])
print("and we merged", merges[first_difference])

998 of the first 1000 merges are the same in both
the lists first differ at merge 339
Hugging Face merged ('р', 'ы')
and we merged ('▁го', 'вори')

Almost all of the first thousand merges are the same. Why does the first difference happen? Rebuild the corpus as both trainers saw it at that moment: replaying the merges that came before it, with our encode_word, gives every word’s spelling at that step, and pair_counts gives the frequencies.

earlier_ranks = {}
for rank, pair in enumerate(merges[:first_difference]):
    earlier_ranks[pair] = rank

corpus_at_that_step = {}
for word, freq in all_words.items():
    spelling = tuple(encode_word("".join(word), earlier_ranks))
    corpus_at_that_step[spelling] = freq

counts_then = pair_counts(corpus_at_that_step)
theirs, ours = hf_merges[first_difference], merges[first_difference]
print("Hugging Face's pair:", theirs, "occurred", counts_then[theirs], "times")
print("our pair:", ours, "occurred", counts_then[ours], "times")

Hugging Face's pair: ('р', 'ы') occurred 11268 times
our pair: ('▁го', 'вори') occurred 11268 times

A tie: both pairs were equally frequent, and the two implementations break ties differently. Same algorithm, same data, a different rule for a coin toss.

The tokenizer is now self-contained. Feed it raw, unnormalized text, and decoding returns the normalized sentence:

messy = "  Он сказал:   «Я не  знаю» - и ушёл…"
ids = tokenizer.encode(messy).ids

print(ids)
print(repr(tokenizer.decode(ids)))
assert tokenizer.decode(ids) == normalize(messy)
assert [tokenizer.token_to_id(token) for token in SPECIAL_TOKENS] == [0, 1, 2, 3]

[466, 534, 29, 619, 185, 269, 664, 5, 557, 318, 2916, 4093]
'Он сказал: "Я не знаю" — и ушёл...'

6. How many tokens?

Why 16 000 symbols, and not 8 000 or the 200 000 of GPT-4o? A bigger vocabulary makes sequences shorter, but it isn’t free. The first layer of the model is an embedding table, one learned vector per token:

\[\text{embedding parameters} = \lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert \cdot d_{\text{model}},\]

and the last layer is the same size again, because at every output position the model scores every token in the vocabulary. Worse, a rare token gets few training examples, so its row is learned poorly. The most famous case is  SolidGoldMagikarp: a Reddit username that was frequent enough in the text GPT-2’s tokenizer was built from to become a token of its own, but that, it seems, almost never occurred in the text the models were then trained on. In 2023, Rumbelow and Watkins found that GPT-3 models, which share that tokenizer, couldn’t even repeat the word back and answered with unrelated ones. The token is still there:

show_tokens(llm_tokenizers["GPT-2 (2019)"], [" SolidGoldMagikarp"])

So we measure both sides: the average number of tokens per validation sentence for several vocabulary sizes, and the size of the embedding table for the model of lesson 2, whose vectors have \(d_{\text{model}} = 256\) numbers.

def tokens_per_sentence(tokenizer, sentences):
    encodings = tokenizer.encode_batch(list(sentences), add_special_tokens=False)
    lengths = [len(encoding.ids) for encoding in encodings]
    return np.mean(lengths)


D_MODEL = 256
VOCAB_SIZES = [2_000, 4_000, 8_000, 16_000, 32_000]

rows = []
for size in VOCAB_SIZES:
    candidate = build_tokenizer(size)
    rows.append(
        {
            "vocabulary": size,
            "embedding parameters": size * D_MODEL,
            "English tokens": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.en),
            "Russian tokens": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.ru),
        }
    )

sweep = pd.DataFrame(rows)
table(sweep)
vocabularyembedding parametersEnglish tokensRussian tokens
2,000512,00010.9311.89
4,0001,024,0009.7110.11
8,0002,048,0008.968.80
16,0004,096,0008.527.97
32,0008,192,0008.277.43
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sizes = sweep.vocabulary
ax.plot(sizes, sweep["English tokens"], marker="o", color=COLORS["enc"], label="English")
ax.plot(sizes, sweep["Russian tokens"], marker="o", color=COLORS["dec"], label="Russian")
ax.axvline(VOCAB_SIZE, color=COLORS["muted"], linestyle=(0, (3, 3)), linewidth=1)

ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
tick_labels = [f"{size // 1000}k" for size in sweep.vocabulary]
ax.set_xticks(sweep.vocabulary, tick_labels)
ax.set_xlabel("vocabulary size")
ax.set_ylabel("tokens per sentence")
ax.set_title("Diminishing returns of a bigger vocabulary")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Each doubling of the vocabulary saves fewer tokens than the previous one, while the embedding table doubles every time. We keep 16 000 symbols. Compare the last two rows of the table: going to 32 000 would save less than a token per sentence in either language, and double an embedding table that already holds millions of parameters, a sizeable share of a small translation model. Models with billions of parameters can afford 200 000 tokens, because next to the rest of the model even a huge embedding table is small. Ours can’t.

The token tax, revisited

Back to where we started, with our tokenizer next to the five from section 1. This time we count tokens on the whole validation set rather than on one sentence:

contenders = dict(llm_tokenizers)
contenders["Ours (this lesson)"] = tokenizer

rows = []
for name, candidate in contenders.items():
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "vocabulary": candidate.get_vocab_size(),
            "English": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.en),
            "Russian": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.ru),
        }
    )
validation_counts = pd.DataFrame(rows)
plot_token_counts(validation_counts, "Average tokens per validation sentence")

On Russian, our tokenizer needs fewer tokens than every model in the chart, GPT-4o included, with a vocabulary a fraction of the size. That’s not because we out-engineered OpenAI. Our tokenizer was trained on exactly this kind of text in exactly these two languages; theirs has to serve code, math and dozens of languages at once. On English we’re slightly worse than all of them, which is the honest price of sharing 16 000 symbols between two languages. A tokenizer is a decision about what to be good at, and for a translator that reads English and writes Russian this one is right.

And the word from section 1, cut by GPT-4o and by ours:

gpt4o_ids = gpt4o.encode(" недопонимание").ids
gpt4o_pieces = [gpt4o.decode([token_id]) for token_id in gpt4o_ids]
our_pieces = tokenizer.encode("недопонимание").tokens

token_chips([gpt4o_pieces, our_pieces], labels=["GPT-4o", "ours"])
plt.show()

Save and publish

The tokenizer is one JSON file. Saving it and loading it back must give the same tokens:

TOKENIZER_PATH = WORK_DIR / "tokenizer.json"
tokenizer.save(str(TOKENIZER_PATH))

reloaded = Tokenizer.from_file(str(TOKENIZER_PATH))
assert reloaded.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).ids == tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).ids

The next lessons download the tokenizer and the three splits from the Hugging Face Hub, so that every lesson can start on its own. The course’s copies are published from this notebook. To publish your own, set the environment variable TFS_HUB_USER to your Hugging Face username and add a write token as the HF_TOKEN secret (Kaggle: Add-ons → Secrets; Colab: the key icon in the sidebar).

Every repository on the Hub needs a card that says what it holds, where it comes from and how it was made. The dataset’s card:

DATASET_CARD = f"""---
license: cc-by-2.0
language: [en, ru]
task_categories: [translation]
---
# Tatoeba English–Russian, cleaned and split without leaks

Built in lesson 1 of the course "Transformers: from scratch to production":
https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch

- train and validation: sentence-transformers/parallel-sentences-tatoeba (en-ru),
  revision `{TRAIN_REVISION[:7]}`
- test: Tatoeba Translation Challenge eng-rus test set (Tiedemann, 2020)
- NFKC normalization, combining marks removed, straight quotes, one dash
- training pairs sharing a sentence fingerprint with the test set removed
- validation split by connected components of the translation graph,
  so no sentence occurs in both

Sentences from [Tatoeba](https://tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

| split | pairs |
|---|---|
| train | {len(train)} |
| validation | {len(valid)} |
| test | {len(test)} |
"""

And the tokenizer’s, with the three lines it takes to use it:

TOKENIZER_CARD = f"""---
license: cc-by-2.0
language: [en, ru]
tags: [tokenizer, bpe]
datasets: [xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru]
---
# BPE tokenizer for English and Russian, {tokenizer.get_vocab_size()} tokens

Built in lesson 1 of the course "Transformers: from scratch to production":
https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch

- byte-pair encoding over characters, trained with Hugging Face `tokenizers` on the training
  split of xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru, both languages together
- owns its normalization: NFKC, combining marks removed, straight quotes, one dash
- words keep the space in front of them as `▁`
- special tokens `<pad>`, `<unk>`, `<bos>`, `<eos>` with ids 0 to 3

```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

path = hf_hub_download("xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k", "tokenizer.json")
tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_file(path)
```

Trained on sentences from [Tatoeba](https://tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
"""

HUB_USER = os.environ.get("TFS_HUB_USER")
hf_token = env.secret("HF_TOKEN")

if HUB_USER and hf_token:
    from huggingface_hub import HfApi

    api = HfApi(token=hf_token)
    data_repo = f"{HUB_USER}/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru"
    tokenizer_repo = f"{HUB_USER}/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k"

    api.create_repo(data_repo, repo_type="dataset", exist_ok=True)
    for name in splits:
        api.upload_file(
            path_or_fileobj=str(DATA_DIR / f"{name}.parquet"),
            path_in_repo=f"data/{name}.parquet",
            repo_id=data_repo,
            repo_type="dataset",
        )
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=DATASET_CARD.encode(),
        path_in_repo="README.md",
        repo_id=data_repo,
        repo_type="dataset",
    )

    api.create_repo(tokenizer_repo, exist_ok=True)
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=str(TOKENIZER_PATH),
        path_in_repo="tokenizer.json",
        repo_id=tokenizer_repo,
    )
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=TOKENIZER_CARD.encode(),
        path_in_repo="README.md",
        repo_id=tokenizer_repo,
    )
    print("published", data_repo, "and", tokenizer_repo)
else:
    print("not publishing; lesson 2 downloads the course's copies:")
    print("xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru and xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k")

not publishing; lesson 2 downloads the course's copies:
xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru and xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k

References

  • Gage, P. (1994). A new algorithm for data compression. The C Users Journal, 12(2).
  • Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., Birch, A. (2016). Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. ACL.
  • Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI. GPT-2 and its byte-level BPE.
  • Kudo, T., Richardson, J. (2018). SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer. EMNLP.
  • Petrov, A., La Malfa, E., Torr, P., Bibi, A. (2023). Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages. NeurIPS.
  • Rumbelow, J., Watkins, M. (2023). SolidGoldMagikarp (plus, prompt generation). LessWrong.
  • OpenAI (2023). GPT-4 Technical Report. Appendix C on contamination.
  • Tiedemann, J. (2020). The Tatoeba Translation Challenge. WMT.
  • Heaps, H. S. (1978). Information Retrieval: Computational and Theoretical Aspects. Academic Press.
  • Tarjan, R. E. (1975). Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm. Journal of the ACM, 22(2).
  • Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms.
  • tiktoken, OpenAI’s tokenizers, and the Hugging Face Tokenizers documentation.

Lesson 2: The Transformer →
entry.summary: What GPT-4o actually receives when you type, why Russian costs more tokens than English, and byte-pair encoding written from scratch.

entry.title: Somatic Marker Hypothesis by Antonio Damasio

link.title: Somatic Marker Hypothesis by Antonio Damasio

entry.content:
Why your gut feelings aren’t just superstition — they’re sophisticated neural machinery that’s been running your life all along

Imagine this: You’re sitting across from a charming stranger on a first date. The conversation flows effortlessly, they’re attractive, successful, share your interests. On paper, they’re perfect. But something in your chest constricts with each laugh, each seemingly innocent comment. Your rational mind chides you for being paranoid, but your body whispers warnings you can’t quite articulate.

Three months later, you discover they’ve been lying about everything that matters.

How did you know? How could a collection of cells and neurons possibly detect deception more accurately than your sophisticated conscious analysis? The answer lies in one of the most revolutionary discoveries in neuroscience — and it turns everything we thought we knew about human intelligence upside down.

The Uncomfortable Truth About Your Brain

For centuries, we’ve told ourselves a comforting story about human cognition: that we’re rational beings who occasionally get hijacked by primitive emotions. That the highest form of intelligence is cold, calculating logic. That the path to better decisions lies in suppressing our feelings and embracing pure reason.

This story isn’t just wrong — it’s dangerous.

Antonio Damasio, a Portuguese-American neuroscientist, spent decades studying patients with brain damage, and what he discovered should fundamentally change how you think about every decision you make. His findings, published in the groundbreaking 1994 book “Descartes’ Error,” revealed that emotion and reason aren’t competing systems. They’re so thoroughly integrated that damage to one cripples the other entirely.

The implications are staggering: Your body has been making decisions for you your entire life, often with breathtaking accuracy, and you’ve been trained to ignore it.

The Lawyer Who Lost His Soul

Meet Elliot — though that’s not his real name. Before his brain tumor, he was everything our society celebrates: a successful attorney, devoted father, pillar of his community. His IQ was superior, his memory photographic, his logical reasoning flawless. Then surgeons removed a tumor from his ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and everything changed.

Not his intelligence — that remained pristine. Not his memory — every fact perfectly preserved. What vanished was something far more fundamental: his ability to feel the weight of his choices.

Elliot could analyze the pros and cons of restaurant options for hours, constructing elaborate decision trees worthy of Harvard Business School. He could explain with clinical precision why his wife leaving him was problematic, but felt no grief. He could understand that losing his life savings was financially catastrophic, but experienced no regret, no anxiety, no motivation to prevent it from happening again.

He became a human computer — brilliant at processing information, utterly hopeless at living life.

The cruel irony? Elliot could pass every test of rationality while making one disastrous decision after another. He cycled through jobs, relationships, investments, each failure analyzed with perfect logic but no emotional learning. Watching him was like observing a chess grandmaster who had forgotten why winning mattered.

The Railroad Worker Who Rewrote Psychology

But Elliot wasn’t unique. In 1848, a railroad foreman named Phineas Gage was preparing a blasting charge when an iron rod three feet long and over an inch thick shot through his skull like a javelin. Miraculously, he survived. His intelligence remained intact, his memory perfect, his language fluent.

Yet everyone who knew him said the same thing: “This is no longer Phineas Gage.”

Before the accident, Gage was described as responsible, social, and well-liked — the kind of man you’d trust with your life. After? He became impulsive, irreverent, and socially inappropriate. He couldn’t hold a job, couldn’t maintain relationships, couldn’t make the kind of basic life decisions that any functioning adult manages automatically.

What did Elliot and Gage share? Both had damage to the same brain region — the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. This wasn’t coincidence. It was the key to understanding something profound about human intelligence: we don’t just think with our brains. We think with our entire bodies.

The Card Game That Changed Everything

To test his revolutionary theory, Damasio created a deceptively simple experiment: the Iowa Gambling Task. Participants sit before four decks of cards, each containing different patterns of rewards and punishments. Two decks offer large immediate payoffs but devastating long-term losses — like a predatory loan with attractive terms. Two offer modest rewards but sustainable long-term gains — like a sensible investment strategy.

The participants have no idea about these patterns. They’re told only to maximize their winnings.

Here’s what happens with healthy participants, and it’s genuinely eerie:

Cards 1-10: Random exploration. They sample all decks, trying to figure out the rules.

Cards 10-50: Their skin conductance starts spiking when they reach for the “bad” decks. Their bodies are detecting danger before their minds understand what’s happening. They can’t explain why, but they start avoiding certain decks.

Cards 50-80: They develop strong preferences for the “good” decks, still unable to articulate the underlying patterns.

Cards 80+: Finally, conscious understanding emerges. They can explain the deck patterns and their strategy.

The body knows. The mind follows. By several dozen cards.

But here’s where it gets genuinely disturbing: patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, like Elliot, never develop those early warning signals. Their skin conductance stays flat. They keep choosing the devastating decks long after healthy participants have learned to avoid them.

Even more chilling: they can intellectually understand the patterns when explained, but they can’t feel why they matter. It’s like explaining to a colorblind person that the red wire is dangerous — they can memorize the rule, but they can’t perceive the difference that makes it meaningful.

The Neurobiology of Intuition

So how does this actually work? How can a collection of cells in your gut possibly know things your conscious mind hasn’t figured out yet?

The answer lies in what Damasio calls “somatic markers” — from the Greek word sōma, meaning body. These are subtle physiological signals that your nervous system generates based on past experiences. Every time you encounter a situation, your body runs a lightning-fast simulation: “Last time something like this happened, how did it feel?”

The amygdala, often called the brain’s “fear center,” processes these patterns at speeds that make conscious thought look glacial. It’s constantly scanning for threats, opportunities, and familiar patterns, creating emotional associations that bypass your rational mind entirely.

The vagus nerve — a massive information highway connecting your brain to your heart, lungs, and digestive system — transmits these signals throughout your body. When your stomach “drops” during a stressful presentation, when your heart races before a job interview, when you feel “butterflies” about a big decision — that’s your vagus nerve at work, transmitting crucial information about your internal state.

The ventromedial prefrontal cortex then integrates these bodily signals with abstract reasoning, social context, and long-term planning. It’s where your gut feelings get translated into actionable insights.

Damage any part of this system, and you lose access to decades of embodied wisdom. You become, in essence, a tourist in your own life — able to observe and analyze, but unable to feel the weight of consequences.

The Counterattack: When Science Gets Uncomfortable

Damasio’s findings were so radical that they triggered a scientific backlash. Critics raised legitimate concerns:

The Consciousness Problem: Researchers like Maia and McClelland argued that participants in the Iowa Gambling Task actually had more conscious awareness than Damasio claimed. Maybe those “unconscious” somatic markers weren’t so unconscious after all.

The Specificity Problem: When exactly do somatic markers influence decisions? For all choices? Only complex ones? Only emotional ones? The theory seemed frustratingly vague about its own boundaries.

The Replication Problem: Multiple research groups found mixed results when trying to replicate the Iowa Gambling Task findings. Some studies showed that participants could use pure logic to crack the task, no somatic markers required.

These criticisms revealed something important: the relationship between emotion and reason is more complex than any simple theory can capture. But they also missed something crucial about what Damasio was actually claiming.

The Integration Revolution

Recent neuroscience suggests that the emotion-versus-reason debate has been asking the wrong question entirely. We’ve been treating them as separate systems that sometimes cooperate, like oil and water that occasionally mix. But that’s not how the brain actually works.

Modern brain imaging reveals that emotional and rational processing aren’t competing systems — they’re deeply integrated networks that function as a unified whole. Your prefrontal cortex doesn’t just override your emotions; it incorporates them into a sophisticated decision-making process that includes:

  • Pattern recognition from past experiences (amygdala and hippocampus)
  • Physiological stress responses (vagus nerve and autonomic nervous system)
  • Abstract reasoning about future consequences (prefrontal cortex)
  • Social context about relationships and obligations (various cortical regions)
  • Embodied simulation of potential outcomes (somatic markers throughout the body)

The magic isn’t in choosing between emotion and reason — it’s in their seamless integration. When this integration breaks down, as it did with Elliot and Gage, you don’t become more rational. You become less human.

The Practical Implications: How to Actually Use This Knowledge

Understanding somatic markers isn’t just academic curiosity. It has profound implications for how you navigate everything from career choices to relationships to financial decisions. Here’s how to actually apply this knowledge:

Trust Your Gut (But Verify)

Your initial emotional reaction to a situation often contains valuable information that your conscious mind hasn’t processed yet. That uneasy feeling about a business partner, that inexplicable excitement about a new opportunity — these aren’t random neural noise.

Practical technique: When facing a decision, pay attention to your body’s immediate response before your rational mind engages. Notice physical sensations: tension in your shoulders, flutter in your chest, knot in your stomach. These are data points, not just feelings.

But emotions can also mislead. The same physiological arousal that signals danger can also signal excitement. Context matters enormously.

The verification step: After noting your somatic response, consciously analyze why you might be feeling this way. Are you responding to genuine patterns, or are you triggered by irrelevant factors like the person’s appearance or accent?

The Paradox of Choice

When faced with complex decisions — especially those involving uncertain outcomes and emotional stakes — your somatic markers can help cut through analysis paralysis. They provide a rapid, unconscious filtering system that narrows your options to the most viable alternatives.

Practical technique: When overwhelmed by options, create a shortlist based on your immediate gut reactions. Then apply rational analysis only to your top choices. This leverages your body’s pattern recognition while preserving cognitive resources for detailed evaluation.

Learning from Experience

Every decision you make creates new somatic markers. The anxiety you felt after that impulsive purchase, the satisfaction from that well-researched investment, the regret from that hasty relationship decision — your body is literally learning from these experiences and encoding them for future reference.

Practical technique: After making significant decisions, consciously connect the outcome to your initial somatic response. Did your gut feeling prove accurate? What physical sensations preceded good or bad outcomes? This strengthens your body’s decision-making calibration over time.

The Stress Response Paradox

Here’s something counterintuitive: mild stress often improves decision-making by activating your somatic marker system. But chronic stress or extreme anxiety can overwhelm it, leading to poor choices.

Practical technique: For important decisions, aim for a state of “aroused calm” — alert but not panicked. If you’re too stressed, your somatic markers become noise. If you’re too relaxed, you lose access to important emotional information.

The Modern Twist: AI, Emotions, and the Future of Decision-Making

In our age of artificial intelligence and algorithmic decision-making, Damasio’s insights take on new urgency. We’re building systems that can process vast amounts of data and optimize for specific outcomes, but they lack the embodied wisdom that comes from having a body that can feel consequences.

This creates a fascinating paradox: AI systems are already superior to humans at many types of decisions — medical diagnosis, financial analysis, strategic planning. But they fail catastrophically at the kinds of decisions that require integrating emotional intelligence with rational analysis.

When you’re deciding whether to trust someone, whether to take a creative risk, whether to commit to a relationship — you’re not just processing information. You’re integrating decades of embodied experience, physiological responses, and contextual awareness in ways that no algorithm can yet replicate.

This isn’t necessarily a limitation of AI — it’s a reminder of something unique about human intelligence. Our emotions aren’t a bug in the system. They’re a feature.

The Deeper Revolution

Damasio’s work suggests something profound about the nature of human experience: we don’t just think with our brains. We think with our entire bodies. This has implications that extend far beyond neuroscience:

For Education: Maybe we need to teach decision-making skills that incorporate both analytical thinking and emotional intelligence. Traditional education focuses on suppressing emotions to think clearly, but this might be exactly backward.

For Leadership: The best leaders might be those who can integrate rational analysis with somatic wisdom. They can feel the emotional climate of their organization while maintaining strategic clarity.

For Mental Health: Understanding how trauma affects the body’s decision-making systems opens new therapeutic possibilities. PTSD, anxiety, and depression all involve disruptions to the somatic marker system.

For Philosophy: The ancient mind-body problem gets reframed entirely when we realize there was never a real separation to begin with. We’re not minds trapped in bodies or bodies controlled by minds. We’re integrated beings whose intelligence emerges from their unity.

The Bottom Line: Your Body Has Been Keeping Score All Along

Antonio Damasio didn’t just propose a new theory of decision-making. He revealed something fundamental about what it means to be human. We’re not rational machines occasionally disrupted by emotions. We’re not emotional creatures occasionally guided by reason.

We’re integrated beings whose intelligence emerges from the complex interplay between our bodies, our emotions, and our conscious minds. The artificial separation between “thinking” and “feeling” that has dominated Western thought for centuries isn’t just wrong — it’s counterproductive.

The next time you’re facing a difficult decision, pay attention to what your body is telling you. That flutter in your chest, that knot in your stomach, that sense of lightness or heaviness — these aren’t distractions from good decision-making. They’re part of the most sophisticated decision-making system ever evolved.

Your body has been keeping score all along. Maybe it’s time to start listening.

After all, Elliot could analyze every angle of his life’s collapse with perfect logic, but he couldn’t feel why any of it mattered. Don’t make his mistake. Your emotions aren’t the enemy of good judgment — they’re its most essential ally.

The next time someone tells you to “think, don’t feel,” remember: you can’t actually do one without the other. And that’s not a limitation of human intelligence — it’s its greatest strength.
entry.summary: Why your gut feelings aren't just superstition — they're sophisticated neural machinery that's been running your life all along

entry.title: LLM Inference Optimization
entry.content:
Open the price list of a large model API and compare two columns. On Anthropic’s, an output token costs five times as much as an input token, for every model on the list. An input token the provider has already seen, a cache hit, costs a tenth of a fresh one or less. These ratios are not a marketing decision. They are the physics of a GPU running a transformer, handed down to you: reading a prompt is cheap, writing an answer is expensive, and remembering a conversation takes memory that someone has to pay for.

You can watch the same physics from the other side. I took a model with one and a half billion parameters, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, put it on the free T4 GPU that Kaggle gives everyone, and let it generate text for one user. nvidia-smi reported the GPU 100% busy. The GPU did 0.3% of the arithmetic it is built for. Then I gave it 1,024 users at once. nvidia-smi still said 100%, and this time the GPU did a hundred times more work.

Inference optimization lives in the gap between these two runs. Below, in order: what a request does on the GPU, why generating text is limited by memory rather than by arithmetic, where the memory goes, and what serving engines such as vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM do about each part. Then the system around the engine: streaming, queues, scaling and the numbers to watch. Every measurement comes from one script that runs on the same free GPU, and every figure is drawn from its output by code you can rerun.

Two phases of one request

A request starts with a prompt. The engine turns it into tokens and runs the model over all of them in a single forward pass. This is the prefill: every layer computes keys and values for every prompt token, in parallel, and the last position yields the probabilities of the first new token. Then comes the decode: the model takes the token it has just produced, runs one more forward pass and gets the next one. One token per pass, each pass waiting for the one before it, until an end-of-sequence token or the length limit.

In code the two phases are the same model(...) call. On the hardware they behave nothing alike. Here is one request on the T4, drawn to scale: a 1,024-token prompt and a 64-token answer.

Reading the prompt took 275 ms, about 3,700 tokens per second. Each token of the answer took 37 ms, 27 tokens per second. The answer is sixteen times shorter than the prompt and took eight times longer.

Two numbers describe how fast a request feels, one per phase:

  • Time to first token (TTFT): the wait before anything appears. It is the time in the queue plus the prefill, so it grows with the prompt.
  • Time per output token (TPOT), also called inter-token latency: the pace of the stream after that. It is one decoding step.

A third number describes the service rather than one user: throughput, tokens per second over all requests together. The DistServe paper adds a fourth, closer to what a business wants: goodput, the request rate a GPU can serve while keeping, say, 90% of requests within their TTFT and TPOT targets. A server can raise its throughput by making everyone wait. Goodput doesn’t let it.

The price list now reads differently. An input token goes through the prefill together with thousands of others. An output token gets a forward pass of its own. The next section is about why that pass costs so much.

Why decoding is slow: the memory wall

A GPU has two resources that matter here. It does arithmetic, measured in floating-point operations per second, and it moves data between its memory and its compute units, measured in bytes per second. From the datasheets:

GPU 16-bit tensor math memory bandwidth FLOPs per byte to stay busy
T4 65 TFLOPS 320 GB/s 203
A100 80GB SXM 312 TFLOPS 2,039 GB/s 153
H100 SXM 989 TFLOPS 3,350 GB/s 295

The A100 and H100 pages print 624 and 1,979 TFLOPS. Those figures assume structured sparsity, which a dense model doesn’t use; without it the throughput is half.

The last column is the ratio of the other two, the ridge point. A kernel that does fewer operations per byte it reads than the ridge point waits for memory, however many TFLOPS the GPU has. A kernel that does more waits for arithmetic.

Now count for one decoding step. A weight matrix \(W\) of shape \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\) is applied to \(B\) token vectors, one for each sequence in the batch. Each output number takes \(d_{\text{in}}\) multiplications and as many additions, so the step does \(2 B d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}\) operations. To do them, the GPU reads the matrix from memory once: \(2 d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}\) bytes in 16-bit precision. The inputs and outputs are \(B\) short vectors and small next to the matrix. The arithmetic intensity, operations per byte, is

\[I = \frac{2 B \, d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}}{2 \, d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}} = B .\]

One sequence, one operation per byte. The H100 needs 295 to keep its tensor cores busy, so decoding a single sequence can use at most a third of a percent of its arithmetic.

The roofline model puts both limits into one bound. A step that reads \(M\) bytes and does \(F\) operations takes at least

\[t \;\ge\; \max\left(\frac{M}{\text{bandwidth}},\; \frac{F}{\text{peak}}\right).\]

The first term is the time to read the data, the second the time to compute on it. The larger one is the bottleneck, and speeding up the other changes nothing. Drawn as attainable FLOP/s against intensity, the bound is a slope that turns flat at the ridge point:

The dots are the T4, measured: every weight matrix of Qwen2.5-1.5B applied to a batch of 1 to 2,048 new tokens, recorded as a CUDA graph so that the timing holds GPU work only (more on that below). They climb the slope and bend where the roofline says they should, below it. Measured memory bandwidth peaked at 224 GB/s, 70% of the datasheet’s 320, and the arithmetic at 22 TFLOP/s, a third of 65. During the run the T4 sat at its 70 W power limit, and nvidia-smi showed its clock at 600 to 800 MHz. Datasheet numbers are ceilings; plan with measured ones.

In time per step the same measurement looks like this:

One step for one sequence took 15 ms. For 64 sequences it took 20 ms. Sixty-three more users cost 30% more time, because the expensive part, reading 3.1 GB of weights, happens once per step whatever the batch. From about 256 sequences on the step is compute-bound, its time grows in proportion to the batch, and the throughput levels off at about 7,000 tokens per second.

This is the central fact of serving language models. A single sequence leaves almost all of a GPU’s arithmetic unused, and the way to use it is to decode many sequences in the same step. Most of what follows is about making large batches possible: fitting their memory, keeping them full, and not letting one request hold up the rest.

The same fact gives a ceiling you can compute before renting anything. One sequence can’t decode faster than the GPU reads all the weights:

def decode_ceiling(params, bytes_per_param, bandwidth):
    # every decoding step reads every weight once
    return bandwidth / (params * bytes_per_param)

print(f"{decode_ceiling(8.03e9, 2, 3.35e12):.0f} tokens/s")  # Llama 3.1 8B, bf16, one H100

209 tokens/s

Real engines land below it: attention adds the reads of the KV cache, and no kernel reaches the datasheet’s bandwidth.

What nvidia-smi measures. Its GPU-Util is, in NVIDIA’s words, the “percent of time over the past sample period during which one or more kernels was executing on the GPU”. It counts time, not work. A kernel that streams weights at full bandwidth while the tensor cores stand idle counts as 100%. In the same runs another column of nvidia-smi, memory utilization, the share of time memory was being read or written, was closer to the truth: 100% for one sequence, 36% for 1,024. To see how much of the chip is working, use the profiling metrics of DCGM: DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE, DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE, “the fraction of cycles the tensor (HMMA / IMMA) pipe was active”, and DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE.

What Python costs. The same decoding step run by transformers the usual way, eagerly, took 37 ms instead of 15: the red dot on the right. The model and the kernels are the same. The difference is that Python launches hundreds of small kernels one after another, and with one sequence the GPU finishes each before the next one arrives. Serving engines record the decoding step once as a CUDA graph and replay the whole step with a single launch; vLLM does it by default, for a range of batch sizes. On a small model the launches can cost more than the math.

The KV cache: what the model has to remember

Attention lets a new token look at every token before it, and for that it needs their keys and values in every layer. Those don’t change once computed, since a causal model never lets an early token see a later one, so the engine keeps them. This store is the KV cache. Without it, every decoding step would process the whole text from the beginning. Here is the same 1,024-token answer generated both ways:

With the cache, every step costs the same 37 ms. Without it, step \(t\) processes all \(t\) tokens again, and the answer takes 160 seconds instead of 38. The cache trades that compute for memory, and memory is what runs out.

How much memory? Every layer stores one key and one value vector per KV head, for every token:

\[\text{bytes per token} = 2 \cdot L \cdot H_{kv} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b ,\]

where the 2 counts keys and values, \(L\) is the number of layers, \(H_{kv}\) the number of key-value heads, \(d_{\text{head}}\) the size of a head, and \(b\) the bytes per number, 2 in bf16. For Llama 3.1 70B that is \(2 \cdot 80 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 327{,}680\) bytes, 320 KiB for every token of every conversation. One conversation at the model’s full 128K context takes 40 GiB, half of an H100.

The formula needs nothing but the model’s config.json:

import json
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

def kv_bytes_per_token(config, bytes_per_value=2):
    layers = config["num_hidden_layers"]
    if "kv_lora_rank" in config:  # MLA: one compressed vector plus the key's positional part
        per_layer = config["kv_lora_rank"] + config["qk_rope_head_dim"]
    else:
        heads = config["num_attention_heads"]
        kv_heads = config.get("num_key_value_heads", heads)
        head_dim = config.get("head_dim") or config["hidden_size"] // heads
        per_layer = 2 * kv_heads * head_dim
    return layers * per_layer * bytes_per_value

config = json.load(open(hf_hub_download("unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-70B", "config.json")))
print(kv_bytes_per_token(config) // 1024, "KiB")

320 KiB

The same function over a few well-known models:

Llama 2 7B and Llama 3.1 8B have the same hidden size and differ fourfold. A formula you will often see, \(2 \cdot L \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot b\) bytes per token, is right for the first and four times too large for the second. Newer models don’t give every attention head its own keys and values:

  • Multi-head attention (MHA), the original design: every query head has its own key and value head.
  • Multi-query attention (MQA), Shazeer, 2019: all heads share one key and one value. The cache shrinks by the number of heads, and quality suffers somewhat.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA), Ainslie et al., 2023, the middle ground: each group of query heads shares a key-value head. Llama 3 has 8 of them for 32 or 64 query heads. The authors also show that an existing MHA model can be converted with further training on 5% of its original pre-training compute.
  • Multi-head latent attention (MLA), from DeepSeek-V2: the cache holds one compressed vector per token and layer, 512 numbers in DeepSeek-V3, plus 64 for the part of the key that carries the position. Each head’s keys and values are computed from that vector when attention needs them. DeepSeek-V3 caches 69 KiB per token; with ordinary attention over its 128 heads it would need 4,880 KiB, seventy times more.

About a number that travels with MLA: DeepSeek-V2 “reduces the KV cache by 93.3%”, but that compares the whole deployed model with DeepSeek 67B, and the deployed cache is also quantized to about 6 bits per number. Counting numbers alone, MLA gives 82%: 60 layers of 576 against 95 layers of \(2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128\).

The size of the cache matters twice. It decides how many conversations fit next to the weights, and so how large a batch can be. And every decoding step reads every sequence’s whole cache, which batching can’t share: the weights are read once for the batch, the cache once per sequence. With 16 sequences on the T4:

At 512 tokens of context the cache adds less than a tenth to the step. Past about 7,000 tokens it costs more than the whole model, and at 16K it takes more than two thirds of the step. This is why long contexts are slow and expensive per token, and some price lists say so: Claude Haiku 5.5 charges five times more per input token for prompts over 100,000 tokens.

Paging the cache

How much cache do you reserve for an answer whose length you don’t know? Early serving systems reserved the maximum, as one contiguous region per request, and most of it sat empty. The vLLM paper measured that in those systems “only 20.4% - 38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store the actual token states”. The rest was reserved for tokens never generated, or lost in the gaps between regions.

vLLM’s answer, PagedAttention, borrows virtual memory from operating systems. The cache is cut into fixed-size blocks, 16 tokens by default. A sequence gets a new block when it fills the last one, anywhere in memory, and a block table maps its logical blocks to physical ones. The attention kernel reads the cache through the table.

A sequence now wastes at most the empty part of its last block, under 4% of the memory in vLLM’s measurements. The freed memory becomes batch size, and batch size, as the previous sections showed, is throughput: the paper reports 2 to 4 times the throughput of FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency.

Blocks can also be shared. Several samples from one prompt point at the same prompt blocks and copy a block only when one of them writes to it, copy-on-write, the way fork() shares memory between processes. The paper measured 6 to 10% less memory for parallel sampling and 38 to 55% less for beam search.

The same sharing across requests is prefix caching. When a new request starts with tokens the engine has already processed (the same system prompt, the same tool definitions, the same document), it reuses their blocks and skips their prefill. vLLM finds such blocks by hashing each one together with the blocks before it, and does it by default; SGLang’s RadixAttention keeps the prefixes in a tree. Prefix caching only shortens the prefill and does nothing for decoding (vLLM docs). This is the cache hit on the price list. When you build on an API, put what doesn’t change at the start of the prompt and what changes at the end: a single changed token invalidates the cache for everything after it.

Batching that never waits

Large batches need requests to batch together, and requests don’t arrive together. Static batching gathers a batch, runs it to the end, and only then takes the next. The batch is done when its longest answer is done, so the slots of short answers stand empty while new requests wait outside.

Orca (OSDI 2022) moved scheduling from the request to the iteration. After every decoding step the scheduler can drop finished sequences and add waiting ones, so no slot stays idle while requests wait. What makes it possible is that sequences of different lengths don’t need to be padded into one tensor: the matrix multiplications run over all tokens of all sequences at once, and only attention runs per sequence, each against its own cache. Orca reported 36.9 times the throughput of FasterTransformer on GPT-3 175B at the same latency. Under the name continuous batching it is now standard in serving engines.

In the toy above the gain is 17 steps against 14. With real traffic it is larger: answers range from one word to thousands of tokens, and a static batch always waits for the longest.

Continuous batching brought its own problem. A request joins the batch with its prefill, and the prefill of a long prompt is a long step. Every sequence in the batch waits for it, and their users watch the stream freeze. Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024) calls these generation stalls and removes them with chunked prefill: the prompt is cut into chunks, and each step carries one token for every running sequence plus one chunk, up to a budget of tokens per step.

Decoding steps get a little slower and stop freezing. The paper reports 2.6 times the serving capacity of vLLM for Mistral-7B under the same latency targets, and up to 5.6 times for Falcon-180B. In vLLM the budget is max_num_batched_tokens, and it is the knob between the two phases: a larger budget gives faster prefills and slower decoding steps.

The other way out is to separate the phases. Disaggregated serving runs prefills on one set of GPUs and decoding on another, and moves each request’s cache between them. Each pool is sized and tuned for one kind of work; DistServe reports up to 7.4 times more requests within the same latency targets. The price is moving the cache, which for a long conversation on a large model is gigabytes.

When the cache runs out. A batch grows until the cache is full. Then sequences that are still generating need new blocks, and there are none. vLLM preempts: it evicts a request, frees its blocks, and later rebuilds the request’s cache from its text, which costs another prefill. (The vLLM paper also describes swapping blocks to CPU memory; the current scheduler only recomputes.) A few preemptions at peak load are normal. Many mean the batch is larger than the memory: lower max_num_seqs, shorten the maximum context, quantize, or add GPUs.

How many sequences will the engine hold at once? Little’s law answers it for any stable queue:

\[L = \lambda \, W ,\]

the average number of requests in the system, \(L\), equals their arrival rate \(\lambda\) times the average time each spends inside, \(W\). At 10 requests per second and 12 seconds per request, 120 requests are in flight. If each brings a 4,096-token context to Llama 3.1 8B, their cache takes \(120 \cdot 4096 \cdot 128\ \text{KiB} = 60\ \text{GiB}\). One H100 has room for about 57 GiB next to the weights (see the next section). Such a service hits preemptions at its average load, before any peak.

Fewer bytes per weight: quantization
